newsitem.title: CHINA: Thai debt burden corporate, short-term - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Thai debt burden corporate, short-term - analysts.

text.p: Thailand's debt problem is corporate in nature, and more than US$40 billion in debt will mature in the next 12 months, Bank of America (BOA) said in a recent research report.
Somprasong Land has already defaulted on a US$3.1 million interest payment on a US$80 million Euro-convertible.
Alphatec Electronics, Thailand's largest semiconductor assembler, has also defaulted on the put payment of a US$43.7 million convertible bond that fell due on June 21.
Fixed income analysts in Hong Kong were reported to be very concerned about similar interest payment defaults on other corporate debt.
BOA estimated Thailand's total 1996 debt at US$90.3 billion, of which US$31.5 billion consisted of loans made under the Bangkok International Banking Facility (BIBF).
Established in 1993, this system allowed certain banks in Bangkok to borrow cheap U.S. dollars and lend in baht, which carried a much higher interest.
The fixed exchange rate protected the banks from currency losses when they switched between the two currencies.
Most of the BIBF debt is short-term at less than one year, and virtually all of it is denominated in U.S. dollars.
During 1993-96, banks were key issuers of external debt, with nearly 38 percent of the total, followed by finance companies with 20 percent and property companies with 10 percent, BOA said.

"It follows that property and financial companies, which general consensus indicates are the financially weakest sectors, are also obvious candidates to either default or need to renegotiate their obligations," BOA said.
Estimates of loans coming due in the net 12 months vary widely, but BOA estimated total debt maturing over the next 12 months at US$40 billion, including BIBF debt.
